passages.where: Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees do their deeds to be seen, and love the best seats at banquets and synagogues, the greetings in the marketplace and the title Rabbi. The site's note says the list moves from private feasts to public worship to the street, every place a person can be seen, and that the love of rank is a temptation for every religious leader, not a peculiarity of the first century. The plain note says the warning lands first on those who teach and lead in his church today.

Watching guests choose the places of honor, Jesus tells them to take the last place and let the host move them up, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. The site's plain note says this is not a clever way to get honor in the end; honor is God's to give, and the humble person has stopped keeping score. It adds that humility is not thinking yourself worthless: the host calls the one in the last seat Friend.

When James and John ask for the seats beside his throne, Jesus says that among his followers whoever wants to be great must be a servant, for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. The site's note says Jesus defines leadership among his people against the pattern of political power. The plain note asks where you could serve this week in a way no one will notice or thank you for.

The builders of Babel set out to build a tower to the heavens so that they may make a name for themselves and not be scattered. The site's note says their sin was not building or cooperating but seeking a name and a security of their own making, and that in the next chapter God promises to make Abram's name great. The plain note asks where you are trying to build a name, and what you fear will happen if you do not.

The elder writes of Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first, slanders the elder and puts out of the church those who welcome travelling believers. The site's plain note says the letter answers by naming the wrong plainly and not answering slander with slander, and that it does not ask anyone to stay under a leader who controls, shames or harms them. It asks whether you have ever kept someone out to keep control.

Asked by the king how to honor a man the king delights in, Haman thinks to himself that the king could mean no one but him. The site's note on the chapter says that, assuming he is the man, he describes a royal parade and is ordered to give that honor to Mordecai. The hunger to be recognized hears every compliment as its own.

God answers the complaint of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe: do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking. The site's note on the chapter says God himself was tearing down what he had built, and that what he promised Baruch was not success but survival. Faithful work in a hard time may never be the kind that is noticed.

The tax collector stands at a distance, beats his breast and asks only for mercy, and Jesus says he, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. The site's note says he compares himself to no one and brings no achievements. The plain note warns that the quickest way to become the Pharisee in the story is to thank God you are not like him, and says the parable speaks first to the church.

Having washed his disciples' feet, Jesus tells them that if their Lord and Teacher has done this, they should wash one another's feet. The site's note says he does not give up his titles but shows what they mean: authority among his followers is measured by readiness to serve. The plain note asks what lowly, unseen, unthanked task you could do for someone this week without being asked.

Paul asks the church to have the mind of Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant and humbled himself to death on a cross. The site's plain note says what he set aside was clinging to the honor and rights that were his, and asks what rights or honors you hold on to tightly. Paul tells the story so that the church will treat one another the way Christ treated us.

misread.taken: Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds is used to justify making sure one's giving, service or devotion is noticed, as though being seen were the point.
misread.says: The site's plain note sets the verse beside Jesus' warning in the next chapter not to perform righteous acts before others to be seen by them, and says the difference is the goal. Here the deeds are seen so that people glorify the Father in heaven; in chapter 6 they are done so that people will praise the one doing them. The question in both places, the note says, is who gets the glory.

whole: Almost everyone wants to matter to someone, and to have what they do noticed. The hunger shows itself in small ways: checking how many people liked a post, rehearsing a compliment, feeling a sting when a colleague is thanked in the meeting and you are not, wanting the title or the office or the seat near the front. In some it becomes a driving force, so that every room is an audience and every conversation a chance to be seen well. In others it hides behind modesty, the quiet resentment of the person who does the work no one praises. The desire is not wrong in itself. What goes wrong is where we look to have it met.

Scripture traces the trouble back to Babel, where the builders wanted to make a name for themselves, and the site's note says their sin was seeking a name and a security of their own making. Jesus watched guests scramble for the best seats, and he warned that the love of the best places, the greetings and the titles is a temptation for every religious leader. Haman heard the king's question and assumed it could only be about him. Even the twelve argued over who was greatest on the way to the cross. The common thread is that recognition from people has taken the place of the one verdict that lasts, so that a person's sense of worth rises and falls with the room.

So the Bible's wisdom reorders the desire rather than crushing it. Jesus tells his followers to take the lower place and let honor be God's to give, and the plain note says the humble person is not playing a longer game but has stopped keeping score. He washed feet and told his disciples to do the same, and the note asks for one unseen, unthanked task this week. Good deeds may be seen, but so that the Father is glorified, not the one who did them. Those who lead hear the warning first, as Diotrephes shows. And those who have been overlooked can hear God's word to Baruch, who was promised not success but his life, and was told to stop seeking great things for himself.

The hope Scripture gives is that the recognition the soul wants most is already offered. The host calls the guest in the last seat Friend. The tax collector, who brought nothing and compared himself to no one, went home justified. Christ emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and God gave him the name above every name, so the way down is not the way to nothing. A person who is known by God and received by him does not need to win the room, and is free at last to make much of someone else.
sit: What good thing could you do this week that no one will ever know about, and what would it feel like to leave it that way?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says verse 1 asks whose glory you are after, and that not to us is a hard prayer for anyone and a good one to say slowly, and often.
